easy.text: What distinguishes a strong acid from a weak acid?

options.text: A strong acid fully dissociates (breaks apart) into ions in water, while a weak acid only partially dissociates
options.feedback: Correct -- strength refers to the degree of ionization, not necessarily concentration.

options.text: A strong acid has a higher pH than a weak acid
options.feedback: Strong acids actually tend to have LOWER pH than weak acids at the same concentration, not higher.

options.text: A strong acid is always more concentrated than a weak acid
options.feedback: Strength (dissociation) and concentration are actually two separate properties -- you can have a dilute strong acid or a concentrated weak acid.

options.text: A strong acid is always more dangerous to touch
options.feedback: Danger level depends on multiple factors, but the chemical definition of 'strong' specifically refers to dissociation, not general safety.

medium.text: Hydrochloric acid (HCl) is considered a strong acid. What does this mean about its behavior in water?

options.text: It almost completely breaks apart into H⁺ and Cl⁻ ions in solution
options.feedback: Correct -- this near-complete ionization is exactly what defines it as a strong acid.

options.text: It doesn't dissolve in water at all
options.feedback: HCl actually dissolves and ionizes very readily in water -- that's central to its identity as a strong acid.

options.text: It only partially breaks apart into ions
options.feedback: That describes a weak acid's behavior, not a strong acid like HCl.

options.text: It turns into a solid immediately upon contact with water
options.feedback: HCl doesn't solidify in water -- it stays dissolved and ionizes almost completely.

hard.text: Acetic acid (found in vinegar) is a weak acid, yet a concentrated sample of it can still be more corrosive than a very dilute sample of a strong acid. Why doesn't 'weak' always mean 'harmless'?

options.text: Acid strength refers to the percentage of molecules that ionize, not the total quantity of acid present -- a highly concentrated weak acid can still deliver a large total amount of H⁺ ions
options.feedback: Correct -- strength and concentration are independent properties, so a concentrated weak acid can still be quite hazardous.

options.text: The terms 'weak' and 'strong' actually refer to concentration, not ionization behavior
options.feedback: This mixes up the two properties -- strength specifically refers to the degree of ionization, while concentration is a separate measure of how much acid is dissolved.

options.text: Weak acids are actually always more dangerous than strong acids in every case
options.feedback: This is an overgeneralization -- the actual hazard depends on both concentration AND strength together, not a fixed ranking.

options.text: This scenario is actually impossible in real chemistry
options.feedback: This scenario is entirely possible and well-documented -- concentration and acid strength are independent factors.

easy.hard: This classification is based on the extent to which the acid molecules separate into charged particles in solution.
easy.medium: This describes how completely the acid molecules break apart into ions when dissolved in water.
easy.easy: This describes whether the acid breaks apart completely or only partly in water.

medium.hard: A strong acid ionizes nearly completely, releasing almost all of its available hydrogen ions into solution.
medium.medium: Being a strong acid means nearly all of its molecules split apart into ions once in water.
medium.easy: Being a strong acid means it almost completely splits apart into ions in water.

hard.hard: Total acidic hazard depends on both the ionization fraction (strength) and the total moles of acid present (concentration) -- a high concentration can compensate for a lower ionization percentage.
hard.medium: Even if only a fraction of the molecules ionize, having a LOT of those molecules to begin with can still produce a large total amount of acid.
hard.easy: Even if only some of it breaks apart, having a whole lot of it to begin with can still make a lot of acid overall.

options.text: Using electrical energy to force a non-spontaneous chemical reaction to occur
options.feedback: Correct -- electrolysis uses an external power source to drive reactions that wouldn't happen naturally on their own.

options.text: The natural breakdown of a substance over time without any energy input
options.feedback: Electrolysis specifically requires an external electrical energy source -- it isn't a spontaneous natural process.

options.text: The process of measuring a substance's electrical conductivity
options.feedback: That describes a conductivity test, not electrolysis, which actually drives a chemical change.

options.text: A method for cooling chemical reactions
options.feedback: Electrolysis is about using electricity to drive a reaction, not specifically about temperature control.

medium.text: In the electrolysis of water, what two products are formed?

options.text: Hydrogen gas and oxygen gas
options.feedback: Correct -- electrical energy splits water molecules into their two component gases.

options.text: Salt and water
options.feedback: Electrolysis of water doesn't produce salt -- it splits water into hydrogen and oxygen gases.

options.text: Carbon dioxide and water
options.feedback: These aren't the products of electrolyzing water -- that reaction splits water into hydrogen and oxygen.

options.text: Only water vapor
options.feedback: Electrolysis actually breaks water down into two distinct new gaseous products, not simply vaporizing it.

hard.text: Why does the electrolysis of water require an external power source, unlike a spontaneous reaction like combustion?

options.text: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen is energetically unfavorable, requiring energy input to proceed, unlike combustion which releases energy
options.feedback: Correct -- electrolysis reverses a naturally favorable reaction (the formation of water), so it requires an energy investment to force it to occur.

options.text: Water doesn't actually contain any hydrogen or oxygen to begin with
options.feedback: Water is chemically composed of hydrogen and oxygen (H₂O) -- electrolysis simply separates these already-present elements.

options.text: Electrolysis and combustion are actually the exact same type of reaction
options.feedback: These are fundamentally different processes -- one requires energy input (electrolysis), while the other releases energy (combustion).

options.text: There is no real difference in energy requirements between these two reactions
options.feedback: There's a clear and fundamental difference: electrolysis requires an energy input, while combustion releases energy.

easy.hard: This process uses an external power source to force a chemical change that wouldn't happen naturally.
easy.medium: This process uses electricity to make a chemical reaction happen that wouldn't happen on its own.
easy.easy: This process uses electricity to break a substance apart into new substances.

medium.hard: This reaction produces the same two elemental gases that originally combined to form the starting compound.
medium.medium: Water is made of two elements combined together -- electrolysis splits it back into those two gases.
medium.easy: Water is made of two gases combined -- electrolysis splits it back into those two gases.

hard.hard: Since forming water from hydrogen and oxygen releases energy, the reverse process (splitting water) requires an equivalent energy investment to proceed against the natural thermodynamic tendency.
hard.medium: Since making water in the first place releases energy, breaking it back apart requires putting that energy back in.
hard.easy: Since making water releases energy, breaking it back apart requires putting energy back in.

easy.text: What does the octet rule generally describe?

options.text: Atoms tend to bond in ways that give them 8 electrons in their outermost shell
options.feedback: Correct -- having a full outer shell of 8 electrons (like noble gases) is a particularly stable configuration.

options.text: Atoms always have exactly 8 protons
options.feedback: The octet rule is about outer-shell electrons, not a fixed proton count for all atoms.

options.text: All molecules contain exactly 8 atoms
options.feedback: The octet rule concerns electron count around a single atom, not the total number of atoms in a molecule.

options.text: Atoms can only form 8 bonds maximum
options.feedback: This isn't what the octet rule states -- it's specifically about the outer electron shell reaching a count of 8.

medium.text: Why do atoms tend to follow the octet rule when forming bonds?

options.text: Having 8 valence electrons mimics the highly stable electron configuration of noble gases
options.feedback: Correct -- noble gases are especially unreactive because they already have a full outer shell, and other atoms 'aim' for this same stability.

options.text: 8 is simply a random, arbitrary number with no particular significance
options.feedback: This isn't arbitrary -- it directly reflects the stable electron shell structure seen in the noble gases.

options.text: Atoms are legally required to have 8 electrons
options.feedback: This is a natural chemical tendency rooted in stability, not any kind of external rule or law.

options.text: Because all elements naturally have exactly 8 electrons to begin with
options.feedback: Elements have varying total electron counts -- the octet rule is about the OUTER shell specifically reaching 8, which often requires gaining, losing, or sharing electrons.

hard.text: Hydrogen atoms are stable with only 2 electrons in their outer shell, not 8. Why doesn't hydrogen follow the standard octet rule?

options.text: Hydrogen's single shell can only hold a maximum of 2 electrons, so it follows a 'duet rule' instead of the octet rule
options.feedback: Correct -- since hydrogen only has one electron shell (with a 2-electron capacity), it reaches its own stable configuration at 2, not 8.

options.text: Hydrogen is not actually a real element
options.feedback: Hydrogen is a genuine element -- it simply has a different, smaller maximum capacity for its single electron shell.

options.text: Hydrogen atoms never form any chemical bonds
options.feedback: Hydrogen forms bonds very readily (e.g., in H₂O or H₂) -- it just reaches stability with 2 electrons, not 8.

options.text: This is simply an exception with no underlying scientific explanation
options.feedback: There is a clear structural reason: hydrogen's single electron shell has a maximum capacity of only 2 electrons.

easy.hard: This principle is inspired by the especially stable electron arrangement found in a specific unreactive group of elements.
easy.medium: This rule is based on the electron arrangement of the very unreactive noble gases.
easy.easy: This rule is based on the stable electron setup found in noble gases like neon.

medium.hard: This target configuration mirrors the electron shell arrangement of the noble gases, which are famously stable and unreactive.
medium.medium: Atoms 'want' to have the same stable electron setup that unreactive noble gases naturally have.
medium.easy: Atoms want to copy the same stable setup that noble gases naturally have.

hard.hard: The capacity of an atom's innermost (and in hydrogen's case, only) electron shell is fixed at 2, which caps hydrogen's stable configuration well below the standard octet.
hard.medium: Hydrogen only has one small electron shell that maxes out at 2 electrons, so it can never reach 8 in the first place.
hard.easy: Hydrogen only has room for 2 electrons total in its one shell, so it can never reach 8.

easy.text: In the isotope notation Carbon-14, what does the number 14 represent?

options.text: The mass number (protons + neutrons)
options.feedback: Correct -- the number following the element name in isotope notation is the mass number.

options.text: The number of protons only
options.feedback: The number of protons for carbon is always 6 -- 14 represents the total mass number instead.

options.text: The number of electrons only
options.feedback: Electron count isn't what this number represents -- it's the total mass number (protons + neutrons).

options.text: The atomic charge
options.feedback: This number represents mass, not electrical charge.

medium.text: Carbon-12 and Carbon-14 are both isotopes of carbon. What is the same between them, and what is different?

options.text: They have the same number of protons, but a different number of neutrons
options.feedback: Correct -- isotopes of the same element always share proton count but differ in neutron count.

options.text: They have a different number of protons, but the same number of neutrons
options.feedback: This is backwards -- isotopes of the same element must share the SAME proton count, with neutron count being what varies.

options.text: They have the same number of protons and the same number of neutrons
options.feedback: If both were identical in both counts, they wouldn't be considered different isotopes at all.

options.text: They are different elements entirely
options.feedback: Since they share the same number of protons (6), they are both still carbon -- just different isotopes of it.

hard.text: Uranium-235 has 92 protons. How many neutrons does it have, and how would you write this using the shorthand notation with the atomic number as a subscript?

options.text: 143 neutrons; written as ₉₂U-235 or ²³⁵₉₂U
options.feedback: Correct -- 235-92=143 neutrons, and isotope notation typically shows the mass number and atomic number alongside the element symbol.

options.text: 235 neutrons; written as U-92
options.feedback: This confuses the mass number with the neutron count, and reverses which number goes where in the notation.

options.text: 92 neutrons; written as U-235-92
options.feedback: This incorrectly assumes neutron count equals proton count, and uses a non-standard notation format.

options.text: 327 neutrons; written as U-327
options.feedback: This incorrectly adds instead of subtracting to find the neutron count.

easy.hard: This number reflects the combined weight-contributing particles in the atom's nucleus.
easy.medium: This number represents protons and neutrons added together.
easy.easy: This number is protons plus neutrons combined.

medium.hard: Element identity is fixed by proton count alone; isotopes of that element vary specifically in their neutron count.
medium.medium: Since they're both still carbon, their proton count must be identical -- only their neutron count differs.
medium.easy: Since they're both carbon, they have the same number of protons -- just a different number of neutrons.

hard.hard: Subtract the atomic number (protons) from the mass number to find neutron count, then follow standard isotope notation conventions for symbol placement.
hard.medium: Subtract 92 from 235 to find the neutrons, then use the standard format showing mass number and atomic number.
hard.easy: Subtract 92 from 235 to find the neutrons.

options.text: It contains carbon, typically bonded to hydrogen
options.feedback: Correct -- organic chemistry is centered on carbon-based compounds, especially those with C-H bonds.

options.text: It was grown on an organic farm
options.feedback: This is a common everyday use of the word 'organic,' but the chemistry definition is specifically about carbon-hydrogen based molecular structure.

options.text: It contains no carbon at all
options.feedback: This is backwards -- organic compounds are specifically defined by containing carbon, not by lacking it.

options.text: It is always a solid at room temperature
options.feedback: Physical state isn't what defines an organic compound -- carbon-based structure is.

medium.text: Which of the following is an example of an inorganic compound?

options.text: Table salt (NaCl)
options.feedback: Correct -- table salt doesn't contain carbon, making it inorganic.

options.text: Glucose (C₆H₁₂O₆)
options.feedback: Glucose contains carbon bonded to hydrogen, making it an organic compound.

options.text: Methane (CH₄)
options.feedback: Methane is a classic example of a simple organic compound, built around carbon.

options.text: Ethanol (C₂H₅OH)
options.feedback: Ethanol contains carbon bonded to hydrogen, making it an organic compound.

hard.text: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) contains carbon, yet it is traditionally classified as an inorganic compound. Why is this a notable exception?

options.text: Historically, organic chemistry became defined around carbon compounds with C-H bonds (associated with living things), and a few simple carbon compounds like CO₂ were classified separately as exceptions
options.feedback: Correct -- the organic/inorganic distinction has historical roots and a few carbon-containing compounds (like CO₂ and carbonates) are conventionally grouped as inorganic despite containing carbon.

options.text: Carbon dioxide doesn't actually contain any carbon atoms
options.feedback: Carbon dioxide's chemical formula (CO₂) clearly shows it does contain a carbon atom.

options.text: This classification is a modern mistake that all chemists agree should change immediately
options.feedback: This is a long-standing, widely accepted convention in chemistry, not a scientific error.

options.text: Inorganic compounds can never contain carbon by strict definition
options.feedback: This isn't strictly true -- CO₂ and a few other simple carbon-containing compounds are established, well-known exceptions to this general pattern.

easy.hard: This category of compound is fundamentally centered on a specific element commonly found in living organisms.
easy.medium: This category of compound typically contains this specific element, often found in living things.
easy.easy: This category of compound contains carbon, an element found in living things.

medium.hard: Look for the option that lacks the carbon-hydrogen structural backbone typical of organic compounds.
medium.medium: Look for the compound that doesn't have carbon bonded to hydrogen.
medium.easy: Look for the one option that doesn't contain carbon and hydrogen bonded together.

hard.hard: The organic/inorganic divide originated historically around carbon-hydrogen bonding associated with life processes, leaving a handful of simple carbon compounds conventionally grouped with inorganic substances as recognized exceptions.
hard.medium: The dividing line was set up a long time ago based on carbon bonded to hydrogen, and a few simple carbon compounds like this one ended up as historical exceptions.
hard.easy: This is just a long-standing historical exception to the general carbon-based rule.

options.text: The amount of energy needed to break a chemical bond
options.feedback: Correct -- bond energy measures the strength of a chemical bond in terms of energy.

options.text: The energy stored in a battery
options.feedback: That's a different, unrelated type of stored energy, not bond energy.

options.text: The energy released when a substance melts
options.feedback: That describes latent heat of fusion, a physical process, not chemical bond energy specifically.

options.text: The weight of a molecule
options.feedback: Weight/mass is a separate property from bond energy.

medium.text: In a chemical reaction, is breaking bonds in the reactants generally an energy-absorbing or energy-releasing step?

options.text: Energy-absorbing (endothermic)
options.feedback: Correct -- breaking bonds always requires an input of energy, regardless of whether the overall reaction is exothermic or endothermic.

options.text: Energy-releasing (exothermic)
options.feedback: Breaking bonds specifically requires energy input -- it's forming NEW bonds that releases energy.

options.text: Neither -- no energy change occurs when bonds break
options.feedback: Breaking any chemical bond does require energy input -- this is a fundamental principle of bond energy.

options.text: It depends only on the color of the reactants
options.feedback: Color has no bearing on whether breaking bonds absorbs or releases energy -- breaking bonds always absorbs energy.

hard.text: Why can an overall chemical reaction be exothermic (release net energy) even though breaking the reactants' bonds requires an energy input?

options.text: If the energy released when forming the new product bonds is greater than the energy needed to break the original bonds, the overall reaction releases net energy
options.feedback: Correct -- the net energy change is the difference between energy absorbed (breaking bonds) and energy released (forming bonds).

options.text: Breaking bonds never actually requires any energy
options.feedback: Breaking bonds always requires energy input -- what matters for the overall reaction is the balance against the energy released when new bonds form.

options.text: The reaction must not actually be forming any new bonds
options.feedback: Products always involve new bond arrangements -- it's the energy comparison between breaking old bonds and forming new ones that determines the overall energy change.

options.text: Exothermic reactions don't follow the normal rules of bond energy
options.feedback: Exothermic reactions absolutely follow the same bond-energy principles -- they just have a favorable energy balance where more energy is released forming bonds than was needed to break them.
